results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in September 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The specialty-vs-hyperscaler spread is still ~5–7× for the identical card. What changed this month: the Blackwell B200 floor cracked below $4/hr, Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, and — the twist — AWS actually RAISED its prices while the neoclouds kept cutting. Here's the September on-demand map and the three numbers that decide which column you belong in.

...

The takeaway

- As of early September 2026, on-demand H100 rental still runs about $2–4/GPU-hr on specialty clouds (Vast.ai floor ~$1.49, GMI ~$2.00, Spheron ~$2.01, RunPod ~$2.69, Lambda ~$3.99) versus a ~$10–13/hr median on AWS/Azure/GCP/Oracle — a 5–6× spread for the identical card, essentially unchanged from August.
- H200 held or softened slightly: ~$2.30–2.60/hr at the floor (FluidStack ~$2.30, GMI ~$2.60), up to ~$6.31 at CoreWeave, with Nebius easing to ~$4.50.
- The month's real move is the B200: the on-demand floor cracked below $4 (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00, down from August's ~$4.99), spot near $2.12–2.74, and the provider field widened to 30+. Grace-Blackwell GB200 superchips also started renting by the hour (GMI from ~$8.00, Oracle ~$16).
- The twist: while neoclouds cut, AWS RAISED its H200 capacity-block prices 15% on Jan 4, 2026 (p5e.48xlarge $34.61→$39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- The decision is still utilization, not sticker: a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it's busy or not, and below roughly 40–50% duty cycle a per-token API almost always beats renting metal.

...

If you rent GPUs by the hour, the single most expensive mistake in 2026 is still the same one: paying a hyperscaler's rate for a card a specialty cloud rents for a fifth of the price. The spread is ~5–7× for the identical H100, and a month of price moves didn't close it. What did change: the Blackwell floor finally dropped below $4, the Grace-Blackwell superchips started renting by the hour — and, against the trend, AWS raised its prices. Here's the September map.

...

## The price map (published on-demand rates, early September 2026)#

Every figure below is a published on-demand rate, gathered the first week of September 2026 from public pricing pages and trackers. GPU pricing moves weekly with supply, region, and commitment — read this for the shape of the market, then confirm on the provider's own page before you commit a dollar.

- H100 (80GB) — the workhorse, and steady. Roughly $2–4/hr on specialty clouds: ~$1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), ~$3.99 at Lambda. Spot dips near $1.20/hr. Hyperscaler on-demand: ~$10–13/hr — the same card, 5–6× the money.
- H200 (141GB) — more memory, held or softened. About $2.30–6.31/hr on-demand: ~$2.30 at the FluidStack floor, ~$2.60 at GMI, ~$4.50 at Nebius (down from ~$5.50 in August), ~$6.31 at CoreWeave. Note a hyperscaler quirk: AWS's H200 via capacity blocks (~$4.98/GPU) is actually cheaper than its own H100 on-demand list rate, while Azure's H200 sits at the top of the range (~$10.60–13.78).
- B200 (Blackwell) — the month's real move. The on-demand floor cracked below $4: ~$3.70 at Spheron, ~$3.75 at Packet.ai (the cheapest in-stock rate GetDeploying tracked on Sept 3), ~$4.00 at GMI — down from August's ~$4.99 floor — with spot near $2.12–2.74 and the provider field widened to 30+. The mid-market still runs higher (~$5.50 Nebius, ~$8.60 CoreWeave), and hyperscaler B200 is ~$14–16/hr.
- GB200 / B300 (new this month) — the Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, which they effectively didn't in August: GB200 from ~$8.00/hr at GMI, ~$10.50 at CoreWeave (NVL72), ~$16 at Oracle; B300 (Blackwell Ultra) runs roughly ~$7–18 depending on provider. GB300 is still quote-only.

The headline of the month is a split screen: the cheap end got cheaper (B200 floor $4.99 → $3.70) while the expensive end got more expensive (AWS raised H200 15%). The market isn't moving one direction — it's spreading apart.

## What changed since August#

If you read last month's map, here's the delta in four lines:

1. H100 floor: flat. ~$2 at GMI/Spheron, ~$1.49 at the Vast marketplace floor. But brand-name specialty on-demand firmed — Lambda's SXM rate climbed toward $3.99, so RunPod's ~$2.69 is now a more representative "cheap-but-reliable" number than August's headline $1.99.
2. H200: stable to softer. GMI still ~$2.60, Nebius eased to ~$4.50, CoreWeave ~$6.31. No dramatic move.
3. B200: floor down, availability up. The Blackwell on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70–4.00 and the provider count roughly doubled. This is where a founder's dollar moved the most.
4. The hyperscalers went UP. AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices ~15% on January 4, 2026 (Data Center Dynamics) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades. The premium for renting from a hyperscaler is widening, not narrowing.

The through-line ties back to where the compute money is going: capital keeps pouring into new data-center capacity (Crusoe just raised $3B at a $30B valuation), and that new supply lands first and cheapest on the neoclouds — which is exactly why their floor keeps dropping while the hyperscalers, selling committed capacity and platform, can raise a specific part's price into tight demand.

...

It isn't margin gouging — it's three different businesses wearing the same "GPU cloud" label.

- Discount specialty clouds (Vast.ai, GMI, RunPod, Spheron) optimize for cheap, no-commitment, by-the-hour access. Lowest sticker, fewest guarantees.
- Reserved/contract clouds (CoreWeave, and to a degree Nebius) are built for large, committed allocations. Their on-demand rate is deliberately high because on-demand isn't their product — reservations are.
- Hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) bundle the GPU with a full platform, compliance surface, and enterprise support. You pay ~$12/hr for an H100 because you're buying everything around it — and, as January showed, they'll raise that rate when demand is tight.

...

1. Utilization (duty cycle). A rented GPU bills 24/7 whether or not it's inferring. At 100% utilization, $2/hr is cheap; at 10%, you're paying $2/hr for a card that's idle nine-tenths of the time, and a per-token API would have cost a fraction. Below roughly 40–50% duty cycle, stop renting and call an API. We work the break-even the other direction in Rent a GPU or Call an API?, and the LLM VRAM & self-host calculator tells you whether a model even fits the card before you rent it.
2. Commitment tier. On-demand is the most expensive way to rent. If your load is steady, a monthly or annual reservation on the same card can cut the rate substantially — the trade is flexibility for price. (The AWS increase applied to committed capacity blocks, so even reservations aren't a one-way street anymore — confirm the rate before you sign.)
3. The card, matched to the model. Don't rent a B200 to serve a 70B model that fits comfortably on an H100 — even at a sub-$4 floor. Match memory and throughput to the workload; B200 vs H200 vs H100 for LLM inference covers which card each model class actually needs.

...

On specialty GPU clouds, published on-demand H100 rates are still roughly $2–4 per GPU-hour: about $1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI Cloud, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), and ~$3.99 at Lambda. The hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) sit far higher — roughly $10–13/hr for the identical card. Spot/preemptible H100 can dip near $1.20/hr where offered, with no availability guarantee. The floor is essentially flat versus August; a few brand-name specialty clouds (Lambda, Hyperbolic) actually nudged up.

Did GPU rental prices go up or down since August 2026?

Both, depending where you look — and that split is the story. The low end (marketplaces and neoclouds like Vast.ai, GMI, Spheron) held or drifted lower, especially on the B200, whose on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70. But brand-name specialty on-demand list rates firmed (Lambda H100 rose toward $3.99), and the hyperscalers went the other way entirely: AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices 15% in January 2026. Net: cheap GPUs got a touch cheaper, premium on-demand got more expensive, and the spread between the two widened.

...

Why did AWS raise GPU prices when everyone else is cutting?

On January 4, 2026, AWS increased the on-demand price of its H200 EC2 Capacity Blocks by ~15% (p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU), citing supply/demand — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades, announced on a Saturday. It's a signal, not an anomaly: hyperscaler GPU pricing reflects committed capacity and platform value, not the marginal cost of silicon, so when demand for a specific part is tight, the price can rise even as neocloud spot rates fall. For a solo founder it reinforces the same lesson — the hyperscaler on-demand rate is the most expensive way to rent, and you pay it for the platform, not the card.

results.title: Vultr GPU pricing changes and market comparisons - TechNewsDaily - Technology News & Reviews
results.author: Technewsdaily
highlights:
Vultr maintains the lowest market rate for GH200 at $1.99 per hour, outperforming Spheron. While Spheron offers cheaper A100 PCIe rates, Vultr provides significant savings through 1-year prepaid A100 terms and 3-year committed-use contracts for dedicated access.

...

This price remains the lowest in the current market comparison. DeployBase tracks the 8x HGX H100 80GB bare metal server at $23.92 per hour. This total equals $2.99 per GPU-hour. ComputePrices lists a different H100 SXM rate at $2.30 per GPU-hour. Which figure represents the true cost for an H100? Vultr also sells A100 80GB PCIe instances at $2.397 per hour. This configuration includes 24 vCPUs and 80GB of system RAM. A 1-year prepaid term for an A100 PCIe instance at $2.397 per hour drops the cost to $1.80 per hour, which creates an estimated $5,230 in annual savings at full-time utilization. The A100 SXM rate is $2.60 per hour. This premium covers NVLink interconnect and higher inter-GPU bandwidth. The lineup also includes A40 at $1.86 per hour and A16 at $0.51 per hour. Vultr provides several A16 configurations, including 4-GPU setups at $0.512 per hour and 16-GPU setups at $0.574 per hour. As of December 2025, preemptible AMD MI325X and MI355X plans exist. Users can also secure up to 35% savings on dedicated access with 3-year GPU committed-use contracts.

## Market comparisons

Spheron undercuts Vultr on A100 prices.

The Spheron on-demand PCIe rate is $1.82 per hour.

Vultr’s A100 PCIe rate is $2.397 per hour. Vultr wins on GH200. The Vultr GH200 rate is $1.99 per hour while Spheron lists it at $3.02 per hour. Spheron provides H100 spot instances at $2.21 per hour for PCIe. This price beats Vultr’s bare-metal per-GPU rate. Vultr lacks a published spot tier for H100. Vultr also lacks a PCIe H100 SKU. The Vultr H100 bare metal node edges out Spheron by 12% on on-demand rates. Spheron’s H100 SXM spot rate is $2.91 per hour. Spheron’s H100 on-demand node rate is $3.38 per hour, while the Vultr node is $2.99 per hour. You can check live rates.

results.title: The B200 Rental Price Isn't a Demand Signal. It's a Rubin Transition Price. | AInvest
results.author: Oliver Blake
highlights:
Ask what a B200 costs to rent for one hour at the end of August, and the answer depends entirely on which seller you ask. In the tracked market the cheapest listing runs $3.35 an hour and the dearest $16.11; the average on-demand asking price is about $8 an hour, and even the prediction markets now trade a binary contract on where B200 rental prices end the year. That spread — a spot listing under $4 against a hyperscaler on-demand print above $14, a range stretching from $3.35 to $16.11 for the same silicon — is the actual datum. There is no single B200 rental price at the end of August. There is a set of price lists that happen to describe the same GPU, and the disagreement between them is what the market has in place of price discovery.

...

One chip, four price tags.

The mid-2026 tiering of the identical B200 SXM6 makes the point in one table:

| Seller | On-demand ($/GPU-hr) | What the markup buys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spheron | $3.70 | per-minute billing, no egress fees |
| Lambda | $4.99–$5.29 | per-hour, 1x or 8x nodes |
| Nebius | $5.50 | per-hour, straightforward |
| CoreWeave | ~$6.50 | contract, multi-GPU clusters |
| Google Cloud (A4) | ~$4.28 | 8-GPU node only |
| AWS (p6) | ~$14.24 | quota approvals, 8-GPU lock-in, egress fees |

Three months later the aggregates show the same disorder from a different angle: spot averaging $3.86, custom contracts $3.49, reserved $5.86, on-demand averaging $8.07, with the top of the range at $16.11. The GPU is a constant on every row. The seller is the variable — billing clock, node granularity, quota friction, egress line items, margin. An hourly rental quote is a balance-sheet readout of whoever owns the box, expressed in dollars, not a measure of what the compute is worth.

...

Here is the framework the rate cards do not show. A B200-class part costs on the order of $40,000–$50,000 at procurement. Run it 80% of the hours over a five-year life and depreciation alone is about $1.40 an hour. Add the kilowatt-plus it draws, the cooling, the networking, the data-center space, and the interest on whatever money bought the machine, and the honest all-in cost of an hour is closer to $4 — before any profit. Now look at the table again, plus the current aggregates: Spheron at $3.70 on-demand, spot averaging $3.86, custom contracts $3.49. Those sellers are listing below their own replacement cost.

results.title: I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately. | Prashant Maurya
results.author: Prashant Maurya
highlights:
I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately.

Earlier this year, we were seeing H200s at around $1.80/hour. Today, that same capacity is closer to $2.90 to $3.00/hour.

That is a big jump in a short time.

And even at these prices, people are still trying to find capacity.
The bigger issue is not just price. It is availability.

November capacity is already heavily booked. Larger December requirements are getting picked up quickly as well. If you are planning a meaningful training run, an inference rollout, or a product launch, leaving compute until the last minute is becoming risky.

I know every team wants lower prices. We all do.

But right now, I would not bet on waiting for capacity to become easier or cheaper. I would start planning earlier and get clarity on what you may need.

At Spheron Network, we have some exclusive H200 and B300 capacity available for October and November.

If you are working through your plans and want to explore options, feel free to reach out.

results.title: $0.10 versus $0.47 per million tokens: that is the real cost gap between two GPUs running the same model. The GPU with the higher hourly rate turns out to be the cheaper … | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
$0.10 versus $0.47 per million tokens: that is the real cost gap between two GPUs running the same model. The GPU with the higher hourly rate turns out to be the cheaper one per token.

H200 costs $4.96 an hour on demand. B200 costs $7.50, about 50% more. On the sticker, H200 looks cheaper.

But hourly rate is not cost per token. B200 running FP4 processes far more tokens in that hour. Divide cost by tokens processed and the ranking flips. B200 lands at $0.10 per million tokens, H200 at $0.47, a 4.7x gap. We calculated both figures from the source's throughput and pricing data, so check them against your own model.

FP4 is a lower-precision format that lets a GPU do more math per second, at some accuracy cost. That cost is small for most language tasks but larger for math-heavy or vision workloads, so test your model first. B200's native FP4 support is what drives that gap.

- Pick B200 if your workload tolerates FP4 and you want tokens per dollar at scale.
- Pick H200 if you need FP8 or FP16 precision, or B200 capacity is not available.

This is why Spheron runs a marketplace, not a single cloud: H200, B200 and 50+ other GPU models sit side by side on one dashboard, so you can run this math yourself.

Before you rent, check:

- Supported precision (FP16, FP8, FP4)
- Real throughput at that precision, not sticker TFLOPS
- Cost per token, not cost per hour

results.title: The GPU Provider Shakeout: What Q1-Q2 Exits Taught | GPUaaS.com
results.author: GPUaaS.com Team GPU Infrastructure
highlights:
Five to seven are projected to survive ... The mechanism, and what it means for buyers.

...

H100 spot pricing fell to $1.99 an hour during the first half of 2026. That is below the cost basis for providers carrying debt-financed hardware.

Analysis across multiple sources now puts the number of GPU cloud providers likely to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses at five to seven. There are well over a hundred competing today.

Key takeaways

- H100 spot fell to $1.99/hr, below the cost basis for debt-financed providers. Five to seven providers are projected to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses
- A debt-financed cluster breaks even around 70 to 75% utilization. At 70%, right at the threshold, a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster still loses $80K to $130K a month
- Provider stress is visible before any announcement: capacity rationing, slower response for non-enterprise customers, sudden pricing changes
- Vendor-financed providers must price to cover both debt service and the vendor's revenue cut, so an unexplained premium may be structural rather than opportunistic
- Renewals from 2024-2025 land through late 2026 against a changed standard: sovereignty, geographic resilience, compliance, not just access

...

The model itself is simple to state. Sign multi-year take-or-pay contracts for GPU capacity, borrow against those contracts, and race depreciation to the bank. It works when utilization holds and the debt clears before the hardware loses value. The whole art of the raise is arranging capital so the debt is repaid before the collateral decays and before the customer contract runs out. Get that right and a forty-person operator raises hundreds of millions on terms that used to be reserved for utilities. Get it wrong and the facility that funded the growth becomes the thing that ends the company.

◆ A 1,024-GPU H100 CLUSTER, BY UTILIZATION

| Utilization | Monthly result |
| --- | --- |
| 55% | Loss of roughly $330,000 |
| 70% (near breakeven) | Loss of $80,000 to $130,000 |
| 85% | Gain of roughly $340,000 |
| 90% | Gain of $170,000 to $220,000 |

Sources: American Compute 2026 via ModulEdge for the 55% and 85% figures, Spheron cost model dated 4 July 2026 for the 70% and 90% figures. The two models use different rate and colocation assumptions, which is why the bands differ

...

A debt-financed cluster breaks even somewhere around 70 to 75% utilization. On a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster, 55% utilization produces a loss of roughly $330,000 a month while 85% produces a gain of roughly $340,000. Sit at 70%, right at the threshold, and the same cluster still loses $80,000 to $130,000 a month. Push to 90% and it generates $170,000 to $220,000. Bare-metal gross margins run 55 to 65% before depreciation is counted at all.

...

Capital raised in a different interest rate environment came due. Debt service on hardware depreciating faster than model generations is brutal arithmetic, and it does not improve with time. Over a hundred providers were competing for investment precisely when investor scrutiny of unit economics intensified, which meant the capital needed to refresh aging fleets became hardest to raise at the moment it was most needed.

Chip availability shifted the advantage. Blackwell production ramping through 2026 expanded supply, which sounds helpful and was not, for smaller players. Expanded availability makes volume purchasing power and supplier relationships more decisive, not less. A provider without scale loses the pricing advantage that scarcity had been providing.

Hyperscaler price cuts closed the gap that justified the category. Neoclouds existed partly because they were cheaper than AWS and Azure. When the hyperscalers cut, the differentiation narrowed for providers who had nothing else to offer.

...

There is a pricing tell worth understanding too. Providers financed through vendor arrangements carry locked-in cost structures tied to revenue-share terms, so their on-demand pricing has to cover both debt service and the vendor's cut. Providers without vendor-financed capital expenditure can price closer to market because they are not servicing those obligations. A price that seems inexplicably high may be structural rather than opportunistic.

...

Three pressures converged: capital raised in a different rate environment coming due, expanded Blackwell supply shifting advantage toward volume buyers, and hyperscaler price cuts narrowing the differentiation. H100 spot pricing at $1.99 an hour sat below the cost basis for debt-financed providers, which made the revenue side unworkable regardless of operational quality.

results.title: Most teams assume you need a full GB200 rack to beat H200 on inference cost. You don't. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
Most teams assume you need a full GB200 rack to beat H200 on inference cost. You don't.

MLPerf Inference v6.0 results on GPT-OSS 120B show a single B200 GPU running 7,800 tokens per second. H200 manages 3,100. That is about 2.5x, GPU for GPU, before any rack-scale interconnect enters the picture.

CoreWeave leads with its record-breaking GB200 rack numbers, a rack-scale story. This one starts at a single GPU.

The cost gap follows the throughput gap. B200 comes out to $0.073 per 1 million tokens. H200 costs $0.107 for the same million. You do not need NVLink switches or a rack-scale deployment to see the saving, just one GPU.

What this means if you are sizing inference capacity:
- Serving a mixture-of-experts model like GPT-OSS 120B? B200 wins on cost per token at the single-GPU level.
- Already running H200 in production? The 2.5x gap is per GPU, so it holds whether you deploy one card or fifty.
- Waiting on rack-scale GB200 pricing to decide? You can capture most of the saving now.

results.title: Yesterday, we gave $38,000 worth of AI inference tokens to some of Spheron’s most active users, completely free. | Prashant Maurya
results.author: Prashant Maurya
highlights:
Yesterday, we gave $38,000 worth of AI inference tokens to some of Spheron’s most active users, completely free.

For seven days, they can use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at zero cost.
As a founder, my first thought was, why give this away when we could earn revenue from it?

But building a company is not always about maximizing revenue from every opportunity.

Sometimes, you need to give a part of what you earn back to the people who have supported you. That is how you build stronger relationships and a community that genuinely feels connected to the company.

We collaborated with one of our cloud infrastructure partners and decided that Spheron would cover the entire cost for our users.

No hidden charges. No long-term commitment. Just seven days of free access to one of the latest and most powerful open-source models.

We are now working to bring more opportunities like this to our users.
If you are not already using Spheron, I would encourage you to become part of what we are building.
